passages.title: Changed travel plans lead into an explanation of shared work
passages.summary: Paul and Timothy write to the assembly at Corinth and the saints in Achaia. Paul blesses God, who comforts them in every affliction. That comfort lets them comfort others. In Asia they were burdened beyond their strength and expected to die. God delivered them, and the Corinthians helped by prayer. Paul then explains why he changed his travel plan. He was not saying yes and no, for God’s promises are yes in Christ. He stayed away to spare them.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show Corinth, which receives the letter, and Damascus, where Paul escaped.

lds.text: The selected lesson studies comfort received and shared during trials. Why does Paul end his travel explanation by refusing control over their faith?

contextNote.title: Changed travel plans lead into an explanation of shared work
contextNote.text: Paul had planned two visits and did not come (verses 15–16). Verse 17 shows the charge he expects: that he plans lightly. Verse 23 gives his reason under oath: he stayed away to spare them. That could sound like a ruler holding back punishment. Verse 24 corrects it at once. He does not control their faith. He is a fellow worker for their joy, and they stand by faith.

passages.title: Sufficient punishment must give way to comfort and restored love
passages.summary: Paul decided not to make another painful visit. He wrote a letter instead, with many tears. He says someone has caused sorrow to the whole assembly. The punishment given by the majority is enough. Now they should forgive and comfort the man and confirm their love. Paul forgives whomever they forgive, so Satan gains no advantage. At Troas a door opened, but Paul went on to Macedonia to find Titus. He thanks God, who spreads the knowledge of Christ like a fragrance.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show Corinth, which receives the letter, and Damascus, where Paul escaped.

lds.text: The selected lesson teaches forgiveness as a gift both given and received. Why must sufficient punishment give way to comfort and confirmed love?

contextNote.title: Sufficient punishment must give way to comfort and restored love
contextNote.text: Verse 6 says the majority punished the man, and that it is sufficient. Paul does not say the punishment was wrong. Verse 7 says what must come next: forgiveness and comfort. The reason is the man himself. Too much sorrow could swallow him up. Verse 8 asks them to confirm their love for him. Verse 11 adds a second reason: Satan must gain no advantage.

passages.title: The believers themselves become the letter Paul offers as evidence
passages.summary: Paul asks if he needs letters of recommendation, as some do. He says the Corinthians are his letter, known and read by all. His sufficiency is from God, who made him a servant of a new covenant. The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life. The service written on stones came with glory, and Moses’ face shone. The service of the Spirit has greater glory. Moses veiled his face, and Paul says a veil remains when Moses is read. When someone turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show Corinth, which receives the letter, and Damascus, where Paul escaped.

lds.text: How can the believers themselves function as a recommendation letter?

contextNote.title: The believers themselves become the letter Paul offers as evidence
contextNote.text: Verse 1 raises the matter of letters of recommendation. Some carry them to Corinth or from Corinth. Verse 2 says Paul’s letter is the Corinthians themselves. Verse 3 names the author, the carrier, and the material. Christ wrote it, Paul delivered it, and the Spirit was the ink. It is written on hearts and not on stone tablets. That contrast with stone opens the comparison with Moses in verses 7–11.

passages.title: Fragile carriers keep the power distinct from the people carrying it
passages.summary: Paul says he does not lose heart in this service. He refuses hidden and shameful ways and does not twist God’s word. If the good news is veiled, it is veiled to those who are perishing. God has shone in hearts to give the light of his glory in Christ’s face. This treasure is held in clay vessels. Paul is pressed, perplexed, pursued, and struck down, yet not destroyed. He carries Jesus’ death in his body so that Jesus’ life may show. The outward person decays, but the inward is renewed daily.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show Corinth, which receives the letter, and Damascus, where Paul escaped.

lds.text: The selected lesson studies hope and comfort during trials. Why does Paul compare powerful treasure with fragile clay carriers?

contextNote.title: Fragile carriers keep the power distinct from the people carrying it
contextNote.text: Verse 6 describes a treasure: the light of God’s glory in Christ’s face. Verse 7 says where it is kept: in clay vessels. Clay breaks easily, and verses 8–9 list the blows. Paul is pressed, perplexed, pursued, and struck down. The verse gives the purpose of the weak container. The great power must be seen as God’s and not Paul’s. Verse 10 says Jesus’ life shows in a body that carries his death.

passages.title: Restored relationship changes the way Paul sees and addresses others
passages.summary: Paul calls the body an earthly tent and expects a building from God. He groans to be clothed with it, and the Spirit is the pledge. He walks by faith, not by sight, and aims to please the Lord. All must appear before Christ’s judgment seat. Christ’s love compels him, because one died for all. So he no longer regards anyone by human measure. Anyone in Christ is a new creation. God was reconciling the world in Christ, and Paul begs them to be reconciled.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show Corinth, which receives the letter, and Damascus, where Paul escaped.

lds.text: The selected lesson teaches restored relationship with God through Jesus Christ’s Atonement. How does restored relationship change the purpose of the speakers’ appeal?

contextNote.title: Restored relationship changes the way Paul sees and addresses others
contextNote.text: Verse 17 says anyone in Christ is a new creation. Verse 18 says where that comes from: “all things are of God.” God did the reconciling, through Christ. The same verse gives Paul his task, the service of reconciliation. Verse 19 explains it: God does not count their trespasses against them. Verse 20 shows how the task sounds: an ambassador who begs. Paul speaks for Christ and asks them to be reconciled to God.

passages.title: An open heart stands beside a warning about divided belonging
passages.summary: Paul urges them not to receive God’s grace in vain. He says now is the day of salvation. He commends himself by endurance in beatings, prisons, riots, labor, and hunger. He is called a deceiver yet is true, and is poor yet enriches many. He says his heart is wide open to the Corinthians. Any narrowness is in their own feelings. He asks them to open their hearts in return. Then he warns against being yoked with unbelievers, for they are God’s temple.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show Corinth, which receives the letter, and Damascus, where Paul escaped.

lds.text: Why does Paul pair sorrow with joy and poverty with riches?

contextNote.title: An open heart stands beside a warning about divided belonging
contextNote.text: Verses 4–10 list what Paul has borne for his work. Verse 11 then turns to the readers by name: “Corinthians.” His mouth is open and his heart is wide. Verse 12 says the tightness is on their side. Verse 13 asks for a fair return, and he speaks as to children. The same request comes back in 7:2: “Open your hearts to us.”

passages.title: Paul values grief through its changed response rather than its pain alone
passages.summary: Paul asks the Corinthians to make room for him. In Macedonia he had fights outside and fears inside. God comforted him by the coming of Titus. Titus reported their longing, mourning, and zeal for Paul. Paul’s earlier letter grieved them, and for a while he regretted it. Now he rejoices, because their grief led to repentance. Godly sorrow brings repentance, but the world’s sorrow brings death. Titus was refreshed by them, and Paul’s boast about them proved true.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show Corinth, which receives the letter, and Damascus, where Paul escaped.

lds.text: The selected lesson teaches sorrow that leads to repentance and changed conduct. Why does Paul value changed conduct rather than sorrow by itself?

contextNote.title: Paul values grief through its changed response rather than its pain alone
contextNote.text: Verse 8 admits the letter hurt them and Paul regretted it briefly. Verse 9 says exactly what he is glad about. It is not their pain. It is that the pain led to repentance. Verse 10 separates two sorrows: one leads to salvation and one to death. Verse 11 lists what theirs produced: eagerness, indignation, fear, longing, and zeal. By that result Paul judges the grief good.

passages.title: Willing giving must use available means without transferring distress
passages.summary: Paul tells of the grace given to the assemblies of Macedonia. In deep poverty they gave beyond their means for the saints. He urges the Corinthians to finish the gift they began a year ago. He points to Christ, who was rich and became poor for them. A gift is accepted according to what a person has. The aim is equality, as with the manna. Titus goes to them willingly, with two brothers. Paul takes care that no one can blame how the money is handled.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show Corinth, which receives the letter, and Damascus, where Paul escaped.

lds.text: The selected lesson teaches sharing with people in need. How do chosen companions protect the collection from blame?

contextNote.title: Willing giving must use available means without transferring distress
contextNote.text: Paul has just praised the Macedonians for giving beyond their means (verse 3). Verse 12 keeps that from becoming a demand. A gift is measured by what one has, not by what one lacks. Verse 13 states the aim in a negative. Others are not to be eased while Corinth is pressed. Verse 14 gives the aim: plenty on one side meets need on the other. Verse 15 quotes the manna: no one had too much or too little.

passages.title: Advance preparation protects a gift from pressure and shame
passages.summary: Paul has boasted to the Macedonians that Achaia was ready a year ago. He sends the brothers ahead so the gift is ready when he comes. He does not want it to look forced. One who sows sparingly reaps sparingly. Each should give as he has decided, for God loves a cheerful giver. God is able to supply them for every good work. The gift meets the saints’ needs and causes many thanks to God. Paul ends by thanking God for his unspeakable gift.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show Corinth, which receives the letter, and Damascus, where Paul escaped.

lds.text: The selected lesson teaches cheerful giving rather than reluctant action. Why does advance preparation help protect giving from pressure?

contextNote.title: Advance preparation protects a gift from pressure and shame
contextNote.text: Verses 3–5 explain why brothers come ahead of Paul. The gift should be ready as a blessing and not as a forced payment. Verse 7 gives the rule behind that care. Each gives what he has decided in his own heart. Two things are ruled out: reluctance and compulsion. The reason is in the verse: God loves a cheerful giver. Verse 8 answers the fear behind reluctance: God can supply enough.

passages.title: Authority must build the hearers rather than merely win a comparison
passages.summary: Paul appeals to them by the meekness and gentleness of Christ. Some say he is humble in person and bold only when away. He says his weapons are not of the flesh but can pull down strongholds. They say his letters are weighty, but his presence is weak. He answers that he will be the same in deed when present. He will not compare himself with those who commend themselves. He boasts only within the field God gave him, which reaches Corinth. The one the Lord commends is approved.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show Corinth, which receives the letter, and Damascus, where Paul escaped.

lds.text: How does authority’s purpose limit its use against the hearers?

contextNote.title: Authority must build the hearers rather than merely win a comparison
contextNote.text: Verse 10 quotes Paul’s critics: strong letters, weak presence. He must defend his authority and not merely boast. Verse 8 does it by naming the purpose of the authority. The Lord gave it for building them up, not for casting them down. So he can speak of it without shame. Verse 9 adds that he does not mean to frighten them by letters. The same words about building up return in 13:10.

passages.title: Forced boasting becomes a record of weakness and care
passages.summary: Paul asks them to bear with a little foolishness. He fears they will be led astray, as the serpent deceived Eve. He taught them free of charge, and other assemblies supported him. He calls his rivals false apostles. Then he boasts as a fool. He lists labors, prisons, beatings, shipwrecks, dangers, hunger, and cold. Besides these he carries daily concern for all the assemblies. He ends with his escape from Damascus in a basket through the wall.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show Corinth, which receives the letter, and Damascus, where Paul escaped.

lds.text: The selected lesson teaches a simple focus on following Jesus Christ. Why does Paul’s boasting list so many dangers and weaknesses?

contextNote.title: Forced boasting becomes a record of weakness and care
contextNote.text: Verse 18 says many boast according to the flesh, so Paul will too. Verses 22–23 match his rivals: Hebrew, Israelite, servant of Christ. Then the list changes direction. From verse 23 he counts beatings, stonings, and shipwrecks, not successes. Verse 29 asks who is weak without his being weak. Verse 30 states the rule he has followed: he boasts in his weakness. The last item fits it: he left Damascus lowered in a basket (verse 33).

passages.title: The remembered answer redirects boasting toward grace within weakness
passages.summary: Paul tells of a man caught up to paradise, who heard unspeakable words. He will boast of that man but of himself only in weaknesses. A thorn in the flesh was given to him to keep him from pride. Three times he asked the Lord to remove it. The Lord answered that his grace is sufficient. So Paul takes pleasure in weaknesses, for when he is weak he is strong. He says he was no burden to them and will come a third time. He fears he may find quarrels and sin not repented of.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show Corinth, which receives the letter, and Damascus, where Paul escaped.

lds.text: The selected lesson teaches finding strength through the Savior’s grace within weakness. How does the answer about grace differ from Paul’s requested removal?

contextNote.title: The remembered answer redirects boasting toward grace within weakness
contextNote.text: Verse 7 says the thorn was given to keep Paul from being lifted up. Verse 8 says he asked three times for it to leave. Verse 9 is the answer, and the thorn stays. The Lord gives grace instead and a reason: power is made perfect in weakness. Paul’s response is in the same verse. He will gladly boast in weaknesses, so that Christ’s power rests on him. Verse 10 sums it up: when he is weak, then he is strong.

passages.title: A final warning aims to make harsh action unnecessary
passages.summary: Paul says this will be his third visit. Every matter will be settled by two or three witnesses. He warns that he will not spare those who sinned before. Christ was crucified in weakness and lives by God’s power. He tells them to test themselves, whether they are in the faith. He prays that they do no evil, even if he seems to have failed. He closes with a call to rejoice, agree, and live in peace. The last line names Christ’s grace, God’s love, and the Spirit’s fellowship.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show Corinth, which receives the letter, and Damascus, where Paul escaped.

lds.text: Why does Paul pray for right conduct even if he appears to fail?

contextNote.title: A final warning aims to make harsh action unnecessary
contextNote.text: Verse 2 warns that Paul will not spare anyone when he comes. Verse 10 explains why he writes it first. A letter gives time to change before he arrives. Then he will not need to deal sharply. The verse also repeats the limit on his authority from 10:8. The Lord gave it for building up and not for tearing down. Verse 9 shows what he wants: their being made complete.

events.title: Changed travel plans lead into an explanation of shared work
events.summary: Paul and Timothy write to the assembly at Corinth and the saints in Achaia. Paul blesses God, who comforts them in every affliction. That comfort lets them comfort others. In Asia they were burdened beyond their strength and expected to die. God delivered them, and the Corinthians helped by prayer. Paul then explains why he changed his travel plan. He was not saying yes and no, for God’s promises are yes in Christ. He stayed away to spare them.
events.detail: Paul had planned two visits and did not come (verses 15–16). Verse 17 shows the charge he expects: that he plans lightly. Verse 23 gives his reason under oath: he stayed away to spare them. That could sound like a ruler holding back punishment. Verse 24 corrects it at once. He does not control their faith. He is a fellow worker for their joy, and they stand by faith.
events.uncertainty: Markers show Corinth, which receives the letter, and Damascus, where Paul escaped.

lds.text: The selected lesson studies comfort received and shared during trials. Why does Paul end his travel explanation by refusing control over their faith?

events.title: Sufficient punishment must give way to comfort and restored love
events.summary: Paul decided not to make another painful visit. He wrote a letter instead, with many tears. He says someone has caused sorrow to the whole assembly. The punishment given by the majority is enough. Now they should forgive and comfort the man and confirm their love. Paul forgives whomever they forgive, so Satan gains no advantage. At Troas a door opened, but Paul went on to Macedonia to find Titus. He thanks God, who spreads the knowledge of Christ like a fragrance.
events.detail: Verse 6 says the majority punished the man, and that it is sufficient. Paul does not say the punishment was wrong. Verse 7 says what must come next: forgiveness and comfort. The reason is the man himself. Too much sorrow could swallow him up. Verse 8 asks them to confirm their love for him. Verse 11 adds a second reason: Satan must gain no advantage.
events.uncertainty: Markers show Corinth, which receives the letter, and Damascus, where Paul escaped.

lds.text: The selected lesson teaches forgiveness as a gift both given and received. Why must sufficient punishment give way to comfort and confirmed love?

events.title: The believers themselves become the letter Paul offers as evidence
events.summary: Paul asks if he needs letters of recommendation, as some do. He says the Corinthians are his letter, known and read by all. His sufficiency is from God, who made him a servant of a new covenant. The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life. The service written on stones came with glory, and Moses’ face shone. The service of the Spirit has greater glory. Moses veiled his face, and Paul says a veil remains when Moses is read. When someone turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away.
events.detail: Verse 1 raises the matter of letters of recommendation. Some carry them to Corinth or from Corinth. Verse 2 says Paul’s letter is the Corinthians themselves. Verse 3 names the author, the carrier, and the material. Christ wrote it, Paul delivered it, and the Spirit was the ink. It is written on hearts and not on stone tablets. That contrast with stone opens the comparison with Moses in verses 7–11.
events.uncertainty: Markers show Corinth, which receives the letter, and Damascus, where Paul escaped.

lds.text: How can the believers themselves function as a recommendation letter?

events.title: Fragile carriers keep the power distinct from the people carrying it
events.summary: Paul says he does not lose heart in this service. He refuses hidden and shameful ways and does not twist God’s word. If the good news is veiled, it is veiled to those who are perishing. God has shone in hearts to give the light of his glory in Christ’s face. This treasure is held in clay vessels. Paul is pressed, perplexed, pursued, and struck down, yet not destroyed. He carries Jesus’ death in his body so that Jesus’ life may show. The outward person decays, but the inward is renewed daily.
events.detail: Verse 6 describes a treasure: the light of God’s glory in Christ’s face. Verse 7 says where it is kept: in clay vessels. Clay breaks easily, and verses 8–9 list the blows. Paul is pressed, perplexed, pursued, and struck down. The verse gives the purpose of the weak container. The great power must be seen as God’s and not Paul’s. Verse 10 says Jesus’ life shows in a body that carries his death.
events.uncertainty: Markers show Corinth, which receives the letter, and Damascus, where Paul escaped.

lds.text: The selected lesson studies hope and comfort during trials. Why does Paul compare powerful treasure with fragile clay carriers?

events.title: Restored relationship changes the way Paul sees and addresses others
events.summary: Paul calls the body an earthly tent and expects a building from God. He groans to be clothed with it, and the Spirit is the pledge. He walks by faith, not by sight, and aims to please the Lord. All must appear before Christ’s judgment seat. Christ’s love compels him, because one died for all. So he no longer regards anyone by human measure. Anyone in Christ is a new creation. God was reconciling the world in Christ, and Paul begs them to be reconciled.
events.detail: Verse 17 says anyone in Christ is a new creation. Verse 18 says where that comes from: “all things are of God.” God did the reconciling, through Christ. The same verse gives Paul his task, the service of reconciliation. Verse 19 explains it: God does not count their trespasses against them. Verse 20 shows how the task sounds: an ambassador who begs. Paul speaks for Christ and asks them to be reconciled to God.
events.uncertainty: Markers show Corinth, which receives the letter, and Damascus, where Paul escaped.

lds.text: The selected lesson teaches restored relationship with God through Jesus Christ’s Atonement. How does restored relationship change the purpose of the speakers’ appeal?

events.title: An open heart stands beside a warning about divided belonging
events.summary: Paul urges them not to receive God’s grace in vain. He says now is the day of salvation. He commends himself by endurance in beatings, prisons, riots, labor, and hunger. He is called a deceiver yet is true, and is poor yet enriches many. He says his heart is wide open to the Corinthians. Any narrowness is in their own feelings. He asks them to open their hearts in return. Then he warns against being yoked with unbelievers, for they are God’s temple.
events.detail: Verses 4–10 list what Paul has borne for his work. Verse 11 then turns to the readers by name: “Corinthians.” His mouth is open and his heart is wide. Verse 12 says the tightness is on their side. Verse 13 asks for a fair return, and he speaks as to children. The same request comes back in 7:2: “Open your hearts to us.”
events.uncertainty: Markers show Corinth, which receives the letter, and Damascus, where Paul escaped.

lds.text: Why does Paul pair sorrow with joy and poverty with riches?

events.title: Paul values grief through its changed response rather than its pain alone
events.summary: Paul asks the Corinthians to make room for him. In Macedonia he had fights outside and fears inside. God comforted him by the coming of Titus. Titus reported their longing, mourning, and zeal for Paul. Paul’s earlier letter grieved them, and for a while he regretted it. Now he rejoices, because their grief led to repentance. Godly sorrow brings repentance, but the world’s sorrow brings death. Titus was refreshed by them, and Paul’s boast about them proved true.
events.detail: Verse 8 admits the letter hurt them and Paul regretted it briefly. Verse 9 says exactly what he is glad about. It is not their pain. It is that the pain led to repentance. Verse 10 separates two sorrows: one leads to salvation and one to death. Verse 11 lists what theirs produced: eagerness, indignation, fear, longing, and zeal. By that result Paul judges the grief good.
events.uncertainty: Markers show Corinth, which receives the letter, and Damascus, where Paul escaped.

lds.text: The selected lesson teaches sorrow that leads to repentance and changed conduct. Why does Paul value changed conduct rather than sorrow by itself?

events.title: Willing giving must use available means without transferring distress
events.summary: Paul tells of the grace given to the assemblies of Macedonia. In deep poverty they gave beyond their means for the saints. He urges the Corinthians to finish the gift they began a year ago. He points to Christ, who was rich and became poor for them. A gift is accepted according to what a person has. The aim is equality, as with the manna. Titus goes to them willingly, with two brothers. Paul takes care that no one can blame how the money is handled.
events.detail: Paul has just praised the Macedonians for giving beyond their means (verse 3). Verse 12 keeps that from becoming a demand. A gift is measured by what one has, not by what one lacks. Verse 13 states the aim in a negative. Others are not to be eased while Corinth is pressed. Verse 14 gives the aim: plenty on one side meets need on the other. Verse 15 quotes the manna: no one had too much or too little.
events.uncertainty: Markers show Corinth, which receives the letter, and Damascus, where Paul escaped.

lds.text: The selected lesson teaches sharing with people in need. How do chosen companions protect the collection from blame?

events.title: Advance preparation protects a gift from pressure and shame
events.summary: Paul has boasted to the Macedonians that Achaia was ready a year ago. He sends the brothers ahead so the gift is ready when he comes. He does not want it to look forced. One who sows sparingly reaps sparingly. Each should give as he has decided, for God loves a cheerful giver. God is able to supply them for every good work. The gift meets the saints’ needs and causes many thanks to God. Paul ends by thanking God for his unspeakable gift.
events.detail: Verses 3–5 explain why brothers come ahead of Paul. The gift should be ready as a blessing and not as a forced payment. Verse 7 gives the rule behind that care. Each gives what he has decided in his own heart. Two things are ruled out: reluctance and compulsion. The reason is in the verse: God loves a cheerful giver. Verse 8 answers the fear behind reluctance: God can supply enough.
events.uncertainty: Markers show Corinth, which receives the letter, and Damascus, where Paul escaped.

lds.text: The selected lesson teaches cheerful giving rather than reluctant action. Why does advance preparation help protect giving from pressure?

events.title: Authority must build the hearers rather than merely win a comparison
events.summary: Paul appeals to them by the meekness and gentleness of Christ. Some say he is humble in person and bold only when away. He says his weapons are not of the flesh but can pull down strongholds. They say his letters are weighty, but his presence is weak. He answers that he will be the same in deed when present. He will not compare himself with those who commend themselves. He boasts only within the field God gave him, which reaches Corinth. The one the Lord commends is approved.
events.detail: Verse 10 quotes Paul’s critics: strong letters, weak presence. He must defend his authority and not merely boast. Verse 8 does it by naming the purpose of the authority. The Lord gave it for building them up, not for casting them down. So he can speak of it without shame. Verse 9 adds that he does not mean to frighten them by letters. The same words about building up return in 13:10.
events.uncertainty: Markers show Corinth, which receives the letter, and Damascus, where Paul escaped.

lds.text: How does authority’s purpose limit its use against the hearers?

events.title: Forced boasting becomes a record of weakness and care
events.summary: Paul asks them to bear with a little foolishness. He fears they will be led astray, as the serpent deceived Eve. He taught them free of charge, and other assemblies supported him. He calls his rivals false apostles. Then he boasts as a fool. He lists labors, prisons, beatings, shipwrecks, dangers, hunger, and cold. Besides these he carries daily concern for all the assemblies. He ends with his escape from Damascus in a basket through the wall.
events.detail: Verse 18 says many boast according to the flesh, so Paul will too. Verses 22–23 match his rivals: Hebrew, Israelite, servant of Christ. Then the list changes direction. From verse 23 he counts beatings, stonings, and shipwrecks, not successes. Verse 29 asks who is weak without his being weak. Verse 30 states the rule he has followed: he boasts in his weakness. The last item fits it: he left Damascus lowered in a basket (verse 33).
events.uncertainty: Markers show Corinth, which receives the letter, and Damascus, where Paul escaped.

lds.text: The selected lesson teaches a simple focus on following Jesus Christ. Why does Paul’s boasting list so many dangers and weaknesses?

events.title: The remembered answer redirects boasting toward grace within weakness
events.summary: Paul tells of a man caught up to paradise, who heard unspeakable words. He will boast of that man but of himself only in weaknesses. A thorn in the flesh was given to him to keep him from pride. Three times he asked the Lord to remove it. The Lord answered that his grace is sufficient. So Paul takes pleasure in weaknesses, for when he is weak he is strong. He says he was no burden to them and will come a third time. He fears he may find quarrels and sin not repented of.
events.detail: Verse 7 says the thorn was given to keep Paul from being lifted up. Verse 8 says he asked three times for it to leave. Verse 9 is the answer, and the thorn stays. The Lord gives grace instead and a reason: power is made perfect in weakness. Paul’s response is in the same verse. He will gladly boast in weaknesses, so that Christ’s power rests on him. Verse 10 sums it up: when he is weak, then he is strong.
events.uncertainty: Markers show Corinth, which receives the letter, and Damascus, where Paul escaped.

lds.text: The selected lesson teaches finding strength through the Savior’s grace within weakness. How does the answer about grace differ from Paul’s requested removal?

Verse 9 shows what he wants: their being made complete.

ancientRoads.title: Appian Way
ancientRoads.summary: The Appian Way joined Rome with Capua and the port of Brundisium. Rome began it in 312 BCE.
ancientRoads.detail: Acts 28:15 says believers met Paul at the Market of Appius and Three Taverns. Both were stops on this road south of Rome.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The road’s course is well known. The line joins its main towns and smooths the bends.

ancientRoads.title: Via Egnatia
ancientRoads.summary: Rome built this road across Macedonia in the second century BCE. It ran from the Adriatic coast to Thessalonica and on to Byzantium.
ancientRoads.detail: Acts 16:11–17:1 takes Paul through Neapolis, Philippi, Amphipolis, Apollonia, and Thessalonica. The encyclopedia article places that trip on this road.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: Milestones mark the road as far as the edge of Thrace. The line joins known towns and smooths the bends.

ancientRoads.title: Via Sebaste
ancientRoads.summary: Rome finished this army road in 6 BCE. It climbed from Perga on the coast to Antioch of Pisidia. A branch reached Iconium and Lystra.
ancientRoads.detail: Acts 13:14 takes Paul from Perga to Antioch of Pisidia. He may have used this road, but Acts does not say.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: Milestones fix parts of the road. The line between the towns is simplified.

ancientRoads.title: Cilician Gates pass
ancientRoads.summary: This pass crosses the Taurus Mountains north of Tarsus. It joins the plain of Cilicia with the high plateau.
ancientRoads.detail: Armies and traders used the pass for a very long time. Acts 15:41 sends Paul through Cilicia but does not name the pass.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The pass is certain. The line beyond it is a broad guide.

ancientRoads.title: International coastal highway
ancientRoads.summary: This major route linked Egypt with the coast and northern Levant. Traders, messengers, and imperial armies used its plains and passes.
ancientRoads.detail: The southern section followed the coast through Gaza and Philistia. Farther north, important branches crossed Carmel and the Jezreel Valley. “Via Maris” is a familiar later name. This guide calls it the international coastal highway. The line follows Iron Age evidence, not a first-century road study.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route from Iron Age evidence, about 1200–587 BCE. This guide has not reviewed a first-century road study for it.

ancientRoads.title: Jezreel Valley–Damascus route
ancientRoads.summary: This branch connected Megiddo and the Jezreel Valley with Beth Shean. It continued toward the upper Jordan region and Damascus.
ancientRoads.detail: The valley and its crossings supported trade and army travel. The route joined the coast, Galilee, Transjordan, and inland Syria. The line follows Iron Age evidence, not a first-century road study.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route from Iron Age evidence, about 1200–587 BCE. This guide has not reviewed a first-century road study for it.

ancientRoads.title: Beth-horon ascent
ancientRoads.summary: This important western route connected the coastal plain with Jerusalem. It passed through the Aijalon Valley and climbed Beth-horon.
ancientRoads.detail: The ascent used a favorable pass through difficult hill country. It served traffic between the coast, the Benjamin plateau, and Jerusalem. The line follows Iron Age evidence, not a first-century road study.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route from Iron Age evidence, about 1200–587 BCE. This guide has not reviewed a first-century road study for it.

regions.name: Judea · Roman province
regions.summary: Rome removed Herod’s son Archelaus in 6 CE and made Judea a province. Its governor lived at Caesarea on the coast.
regions.detail: Governors Felix and Festus hold Paul at Caesarea (Acts 23–26). Acts 12 names an earlier ruler King Herod; historians call him Agrippa I.
regions.uncertainty: The shape joins Judea, Samaria, and Idumea. The province grew after 44 CE.

regions.name: Syria · Roman province
regions.summary: Rome made Syria a province in 64 BCE. It bordered the lands of Herod’s family on the north.
regions.detail: Believers are first called Christians at Antioch in Syria (Acts 11:26). Antioch sends out Barnabas and Saul in Acts 13.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide to the province.

regions.name: Cilicia · approximate
regions.summary: Cilicia lay on the south coast of Asia Minor. Rome took it in 64 BCE.
regions.detail: Paul comes from Tarsus in Cilicia (Acts 21:39). He passes through Syria and Cilicia in Acts 15:41.
regions.uncertainty: The shape shows the eastern plain around Tarsus only.

regions.name: Cyprus · Roman province
regions.summary: Cyprus was a Roman province under a proconsul. Paphos was its capital.
regions.detail: Barnabas comes from Cyprus (Acts 4:36). He and Saul cross the island from Salamis to Paphos in Acts 13.
regions.uncertainty: The shape follows the modern coast of the island.

regions.name: Galatia · Roman province
regions.summary: Augustus made Galatia a province in 25 BCE. Ancyra was its capital.
regions.detail: Paul writes to the assemblies of Galatia. Acts 13–14 places him at Antioch of Pisidia, Iconium, Lystra, and Derbe.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. Pamphylia on the south coast belonged to Galatia for a time.

regions.name: Asia · Roman province
regions.summary: Asia was a rich Roman province in western Asia Minor. A proconsul governed it.
regions.detail: Paul teaches in Ephesus for two years (Acts 19:10). Revelation 1–3 writes to seven assemblies in Asia.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide to the province.

regions.name: Bithynia and Pontus · Roman province
regions.summary: Rome joined Bithynia and Pontus into one province on the Black Sea coast.
regions.detail: The Spirit keeps Paul from entering Bithynia (Acts 16:7). First Peter greets believers in Pontus and Bithynia.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide to the coast lands.

regions.name: Cappadocia · Roman province
regions.summary: Cappadocia became a Roman province in 17 CE. Its capital was a city named Caesarea.
regions.detail: People from Cappadocia hear Peter at Pentecost (Acts 2:9). First Peter 1:1 greets believers there.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. This Caesarea is not the port in Judea.

regions.name: Macedonia · Roman province
regions.summary: Rome made Macedonia a province in 146 BCE. The Via Egnatia crossed it from west to east.
regions.detail: A vision calls Paul to Macedonia (Acts 16:9). He teaches in Philippi, Thessalonica, and Beroea.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. It includes Thessaly and Epirus, which the province held.

regions.name: Achaia · Roman province
regions.summary: Achaia covered southern Greece. Augustus made it a province apart from Macedonia.
regions.detail: Paul speaks in Athens and stays in Corinth (Acts 17–18). Gallio, proconsul of Achaia, hears a charge against him.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. The province’s islands are not marked.

regions.name: Crete · part of a Roman province
regions.summary: Rome governed Crete together with Cyrenaica in North Africa.
regions.detail: Paul’s ship shelters along Crete in Acts 27. Paul leaves Titus in Crete to appoint elders (Titus 1:5).
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple outline of the island. Cyrenaica is not marked.

regions.name: Italy
regions.summary: Italy was the home region of Rome. It had a special status among Roman lands.
regions.detail: Paul lands at Puteoli and goes on to Rome (Acts 28). Hebrews 13:24 sends greetings from the Italians.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple outline of the peninsula.

guides.title: 2 Corinthians: context and evidence
guides.description: Explore the book’s larger concerns through selected passages and relevant evidence.

steps.title: The remembered answer redirects boasting toward grace within weakness
steps.text: Verse 7 says the thorn was given to keep Paul from being lifted up. Verse 8 says he asked three times for it to leave. Verse 9 is the answer, and the thorn stays. The Lord gives grace instead and a reason: power is made perfect in weakness. Paul’s response is in the same verse. He will gladly boast in weaknesses, so that Christ’s power rests on him. Verse 10 sums it up: when he is weak, then he is strong.

chapterMaps.note: Markers show Corinth, which receives the letter, and Damascus, where Paul escaped.
chapterMaps.narrative: Paul and Timothy write to the assembly at Corinth and the saints in Achaia. Paul blesses God, who comforts them in every affliction. That comfort lets them comfort others. In Asia they were burdened beyond their strength and expected to die. God delivered them, and the Corinthians helped by prayer. Paul then explains why he changed his travel plan. He was not saying yes and no, for God’s promises are yes in Christ. He stayed away to spare them.
chapterMaps.limits: Markers show Corinth, which receives the letter, and Damascus, where Paul escaped.

chapterMaps.note: Markers show Corinth, which receives the letter, and Damascus, where Paul escaped.
chapterMaps.narrative: Paul decided not to make another painful visit. He wrote a letter instead, with many tears. He says someone has caused sorrow to the whole assembly. The punishment given by the majority is enough. Now they should forgive and comfort the man and confirm their love. Paul forgives whomever they forgive, so Satan gains no advantage. At Troas a door opened, but Paul went on to Macedonia to find Titus. He thanks God, who spreads the knowledge of Christ like a fragrance.

chapterMaps.note: Markers show Corinth, which receives the letter, and Damascus, where Paul escaped.
chapterMaps.narrative: Paul asks if he needs letters of recommendation, as some do. He says the Corinthians are his letter, known and read by all. His sufficiency is from God, who made him a servant of a new covenant. The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life. The service written on stones came with glory, and Moses’ face shone. The service of the Spirit has greater glory. Moses veiled his face, and Paul says a veil remains when Moses is read. When someone turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away.
chapterMaps.limits: Markers show Corinth, which receives the letter, and Damascus, where Paul escaped.

chapterMaps.note: Markers show Corinth, which receives the letter, and Damascus, where Paul escaped.
chapterMaps.narrative: Paul says he does not lose heart in this service. He refuses hidden and shameful ways and does not twist God’s word. If the good news is veiled, it is veiled to those who are perishing. God has shone in hearts to give the light of his glory in Christ’s face. This treasure is held in clay vessels. Paul is pressed, perplexed, pursued, and struck down, yet not destroyed. He carries Jesus’ death in his body so that Jesus’ life may show. The outward person decays, but the inward is renewed daily.

chapterMaps.note: Markers show Corinth, which receives the letter, and Damascus, where Paul escaped.
chapterMaps.narrative: Paul calls the body an earthly tent and expects a building from God. He groans to be clothed with it, and the Spirit is the pledge. He walks by faith, not by sight, and aims to please the Lord. All must appear before Christ’s judgment seat. Christ’s love compels him, because one died for all. So he no longer regards anyone by human measure. Anyone in Christ is a new creation. God was reconciling the world in Christ, and Paul begs them to be reconciled.

chapterMaps.note: Markers show Corinth, which receives the letter, and Damascus, where Paul escaped.
chapterMaps.narrative: Paul urges them not to receive God’s grace in vain. He says now is the day of salvation. He commends himself by endurance in beatings, prisons, riots, labor, and hunger. He is called a deceiver yet is true, and is poor yet enriches many. He says his heart is wide open to the Corinthians. Any narrowness is in their own feelings. He asks them to open their hearts in return. Then he warns against being yoked with unbelievers, for they are God’s temple.

chapterMaps.note: Markers show Corinth, which receives the letter, and Damascus, where Paul escaped.
chapterMaps.narrative: Paul asks the Corinthians to make room for him. In Macedonia he had fights outside and fears inside. God comforted him by the coming of Titus. Titus reported their longing, mourning, and zeal for Paul. Paul’s earlier letter grieved them, and for a while he regretted it. Now he rejoices, because their grief led to repentance. Godly sorrow brings repentance, but the world’s sorrow brings death. Titus was refreshed by them, and Paul’s boast about them proved true.

chapterMaps.note: Markers show Corinth, which receives the letter, and Damascus, where Paul escaped.
chapterMaps.narrative: Paul tells of the grace given to the assemblies of Macedonia. In deep poverty they gave beyond their means for the saints. He urges the Corinthians to finish the gift they began a year ago. He points to Christ, who was rich and became poor for them. A gift is accepted according to what a person has. The aim is equality, as with the manna. Titus goes to them willingly, with two brothers. Paul takes care that no one can blame how the money is handled.

chapterMaps.note: Markers show Corinth, which receives the letter, and Damascus, where Paul escaped.
chapterMaps.narrative: Paul has boasted to the Macedonians that Achaia was ready a year ago. He sends the brothers ahead so the gift is ready when he comes. He does not want it to look forced. One who sows sparingly reaps sparingly. Each should give as he has decided, for God loves a cheerful giver. God is able to supply them for every good work. The gift meets the saints’ needs and causes many thanks to God. Paul ends by thanking God for his unspeakable gift.

chapterMaps.note: Markers show Corinth, which receives the letter, and Damascus, where Paul escaped.
chapterMaps.narrative: Paul appeals to them by the meekness and gentleness of Christ. Some say he is humble in person and bold only when away. He says his weapons are not of the flesh but can pull down strongholds. They say his letters are weighty, but his presence is weak. He answers that he will be the same in deed when present. He will not compare himself with those who commend themselves. He boasts only within the field God gave him, which reaches Corinth. The one the Lord commends is approved.
chapterMaps.limits: Markers show Corinth, which receives the letter, and Damascus, where Paul escaped.

chapterMaps.note: Markers show Corinth, which receives the letter, and Damascus, where Paul escaped.
chapterMaps.narrative: Paul asks them to bear with a little foolishness. He fears they will be led astray, as the serpent deceived Eve. He taught them free of charge, and other assemblies supported him. He calls his rivals false apostles. Then he boasts as a fool. He lists labors, prisons, beatings, shipwrecks, dangers, hunger, and cold. Besides these he carries daily concern for all the assemblies. He ends with his escape from Damascus in a basket through the wall.
chapterMaps.limits: Markers show Corinth, which receives the letter, and Damascus, where Paul escaped.

chapterMaps.note: Markers show Corinth, which receives the letter, and Damascus, where Paul escaped.
chapterMaps.narrative: Paul tells of a man caught up to paradise, who heard unspeakable words. He will boast of that man but of himself only in weaknesses. A thorn in the flesh was given to him to keep him from pride. Three times he asked the Lord to remove it. The Lord answered that his grace is sufficient. So Paul takes pleasure in weaknesses, for when he is weak he is strong. He says he was no burden to them and will come a third time. He fears he may find quarrels and sin not repented of.
chapterMaps.limits: Markers show Corinth, which receives the letter, and Damascus, where Paul escaped.

chapterMaps.note: Markers show Corinth, which receives the letter, and Damascus, where Paul escaped.
chapterMaps.narrative: Paul says this will be his third visit. Every matter will be settled by two or three witnesses. He warns that he will not spare those who sinned before. Christ was crucified in weakness and lives by God’s power. He tells them to test themselves, whether they are in the faith. He prays that they do no evil, even if he seems to have failed. He closes with a call to rejoice, agree, and live in peace. The last line names Christ’s grace, God’s love, and the Spirit’s fellowship.
